analysis.one_liner: Cuts off funding for U.S. troops in Iraq after March 2008, except for limited counterterrorism, security, and training missions.
analysis.headline: Ten senators — nine Democrats and one Independent — backed the withdrawal bill, but it never received a committee or floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the President to begin a phased withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq within 120 days and made it illegal to keep paying for the Iraq deployment after March 31, 2008. Three narrow missions would have been exempt: targeted operations against al Qaeda, protecting U.S. personnel and infrastructure, and training Iraqi forces. It was referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and never received any committee or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. service members and their families would have gained most directly: all troops not needed for a narrow counterterrorism, base-security, or training mission would have been brought home on a fixed timeline. Taxpayers would have gained from ending funding for the full Iraq deployment, one of the largest single drivers of federal spending at the time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members, military families, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Ordered the President to begin safely moving U.S. forces out of Iraq within 120 days of enactment, setting a firm date rather than leaving the pace of withdrawal to the administration.
Prohibited any federal funds from being spent to continue the Iraq deployment after March 31, 2008, using Congress's power of the purse to force an end to the war.

Preserved funding for three limited missions — targeted operations against al Qaeda and other terrorist groups, security for U.S. personnel and infrastructure, and training Iraqi forces — so counterterrorism work could continue without an open-ended occupation.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and other businesses whose revenue depends on the large-scale Iraq deployment would lose that business once the funding cutoff took effect. Opponents also argued that Iraqis and remaining U.S. personnel would bear the risk if Iraq became less stable after the bulk of U.S. forces left.
analysis.who_pays_short: Defense contractors and war-spending dependent firms

drawbacks.text: The enforcement tool is blunt: a funding cutoff cannot itself guarantee a safe or orderly withdrawal, and critics argued cutting money for the deployment risked leaving troops and remaining personnel exposed if the drawdown was not executed carefully.

The three exemptions — counterterrorism, protecting U.S. personnel, and training Iraqi forces — were written to allow continued operations indefinitely, so the bill would not have ended all U.S. military involvement in Iraq.

Opponents argued that a legislatively forced withdrawal, without a negotiated transition, could leave Iraq less stable and create space for terrorist groups — the very threat the bill's counterterrorism exemption targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit was large and concrete: a binding deadline to bring most troops home from a war that was costing American lives and hundreds of billions of dollars, while keeping counterterrorism and training capacity in place. The real costs are the ones opponents raised — a withdrawal forced by funding cutoff rather than negotiated conditions could be messy, and the exemptions meant the bill would not fully end U.S. involvement. An honest supporter would also concede that a funding prohibition is an awkward instrument for managing a safe drawdown. But the bill was never debated or amended on those merits; it died in committee without a single vote, so no weighing of trade-offs ever happened in public.

outcome.mechanism: It went straight from introduction to the Foreign Relations Committee, which never held a vote on it, and it stayed there until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Feingold introduced the bill with nine cosponsors, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, on April 10, 2007.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Foreign Relations Committee the same day; that was the last action of any kind.
No committee markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the withdrawal deadline and funding cutoff never took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The war continued on the administration's terms: the large-scale deployment and the spending that sustains it were untouched, which left defense contractors and firms dependent on war spending better off. Military families and taxpayers saw none of the relief the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors and the status quo in Iraq

for.name: Russ Feingold
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wisconsin, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and drove it as its lead sponsor

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, putting the Senate's top Democrat behind a withdrawal timeline

for.name: 8 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.role: 8 Democratic cosponsors (Leahy, Dodd, Kerry, Boxer, Whitehouse, Kennedy, Harkin, and Reid)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no action followed the referral

against.name: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the rest of the two-year Congress

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed fixed withdrawal deadlines throughout the 110th Congress; no Republican sponsored the bill and it never reached the floor for a vote

against.name: George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Fought congressional withdrawal timetables throughout 2007 and vetoed war-funding bills containing them, making any version of this bill likely to face a veto even if it had passed

sides.party_line_note: All ten original sponsors were Democrats or the Senate's Independent socialist, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never got far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.note: The funding cutoff would have ended payment for the large-scale Iraq deployment, shrinking demand for contracted logistics, construction, and supply services tied to the war. Industry revenue depended on the deployment continuing, which put its interest against the bill's purpose of bringing troops home.
